Sources: SRC-0155 Elements of design, Compositional techniques; SRC-0153 color schemes

title: Manlilikha ng Bayan Act (RA 7355)
md:
The **Manlilikha ng Bayan Act (RA 7355, 1992)** honors traditional folk artists whose skills keep a community's art alive. A **Manlilikha ng Bayan** is a Filipino, or group, practicing a traditional art uniquely Filipino at a very high level and passing it on to the present generation.

Candidates must meet five criteria: **technical and creative skill**, **artistic quality**, **community tradition** (they have taught or will teach others), a **folk art tradition documented for at least 50 years**, and **character and integrity**.

Awardees receive a plaque or medal, **₱100,000 at first and ₱10,000 a month for life**, documentation of their works, and possibly a vocational course built on their methods and a DTI study to turn their art into a **cottage industry**. The award is run by the **NCCA** and follows UNESCO's idea of Living Human Treasures. Categories include weaving, carving, pottery, fiber arts and, since 2020, ethnomedicine.
Memory aid: "Skill, Art, Teach, 50 years, Character — and ₱10,000 a month for life."
Sources: SRC-0048 Secs. 3–5; SRC-0170 History, Categories

title: GAMABA awardees in crafts
md:
Many Manlilikha ng Bayan awardees are weavers and makers of everyday objects. Pairing the person, the craft and the place is a common exam task.
- **Lang Dulay**, T'boli of Lake Sebu, South Cotabato (1998): **t'nalak** abaca-ikat weaving.
- **Salinta Monon**, Tagabawa-Bagobo of Davao del Sur (1998): abaca-ikat weaving.
- **Darhata Sawabi**, Tausug of Sulu (2004): **pis syabit** weaving.
- **Haja Amina Appi**, Sama of Tawi-Tawi (2004): master **mat** weaver.
- **Eduardo Mutuc**, Kapampangan of Apalit, Pampanga (2004): **pinukpuk** bronze and silver metalwork.
- **Magdalena Gamayo**, Ilocano of Pinili, Ilocos Norte (2012): **inabel** weaving.
- **Teofilo Garcia** of San Quintin, Abra (2012): **tabungaw** native headgear.
- **Ambalang Ausalin**, Yakan of Lamitan, Basilan (2016): **tennun** tapestry weaving.
- **Ginaw Bilog**, Hanunuo Mangyan of Mindoro (1993): Mangyan script and poetry on bamboo.
Memory aid: "Lang–t'nalak, Magdalena–abel, Ambalang–Yakan, Eduardo–metal, Haja–mats."
Sources: SRC-0170 Recipients

title: National Cultural Heritage Act (RA 10066)
md:
The **National Cultural Heritage Act (RA 10066)** protects what makes Filipinos who they are. **Cultural property** means all products of human creativity by which a people and a nation reveal their identity, whether **movable or immovable, tangible or intangible**, public or private.

**Intangible cultural heritage** covers practices, knowledge and skills that communities recognize as their heritage: oral traditions and languages, performing arts, rituals and festivals, knowledge about nature, and **traditional craftsmanship**. So the skill of weaving t'nalak is heritage, not only the cloth.

The law grades important items. A **National Cultural Treasure** is unique, of outstanding value, and **officially declared** by the proper agency. An **Important Cultural Property** has exceptional significance, as determined by the National Museum or the National Historical Institute.

The **NCCA** leads, working with the National Museum, National Library, NHI, National Archives, Cultural Center of the Philippines and Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino.
Memory aid: "Tangible or intangible — if it shows who we are, it is cultural property."
Sources: SRC-0049 Sec. 3

title: Banig, capiz and crafts as livelihood
md:
Everyday crafts are also local industries. The **banig** is a handwoven mat for sleeping or sitting, usually made of **pandan or sedge leaves**, and in some places of buri palm, reed or rattan. The leaves are dried, often dyed, cut into strips and woven into colorful patterns. The Waray of **Basey, Samar** are known for banig woven from **tikog**. Long ago, pandan mats even served as boat sails.

**Capiz shell** comes from the windowpane oyster. Its thin, translucent shell has long been used as a **substitute for glass** in windows and is now made into lamps, lanterns and decor.

Crafts like these support families and towns. The Manlilikha ng Bayan law itself provides for vocational courses based on master artists' methods and for studies on turning their art into **cottage industries**. In class, DIY projects can use these local materials.
Memory aid: "Banig from pandan, windows from capiz, income from craft."
Sources: SRC-0173 lead, Regional styles; SRC-0176 lead; SRC-0048 Sec. 5

title: Regional weaving traditions
md:
Philippine weaving changes with place and fiber.

**T'nalak** belongs to the **T'boli** of Lake Sebu, **South Cotabato**. It is woven from **abacá** fibers, resist-dyed with the **ikat** technique, on a **backstrap loom**. The women weavers say they receive the designs **in dreams** from Fu Dalu, the goddess of abacá, so they are called dreamweavers and the patterns cannot be mass-produced.

**Inabel** or abel is the **Ilocano** cotton cloth of the **Ilocos Region and Abra**, woven on hardwood pedal looms. It is soft, durable and suited to hot weather. The binakul or whirlwind pattern was believed to confuse evil spirits.

**Piña** is sheer cloth from **pineapple leaves**, especially in **Aklan**, whose handloom weaving is on the UNESCO intangible heritage list. **Abacá**, or Manila hemp, comes from a banana relative found only in the Philippines and also makes rope and fabric.
Memory aid: "South Cotabato dreams in abacá; Ilocos weaves cotton; Aklan weaves pineapple."
Sources: SRC-0171 lead; SRC-0172 lead, Description; SRC-0142 lead; SRC-0143 lead

title: Taking body measurements
md:
A pattern can only fit if the measurements are right, so TESDA's dressmaking standard treats measuring as its own element. Prepare the measuring tools first: **tape measure, hip curve rule, L-square and meter stick**. Then take the client's measurements **in a fixed sequence and position**, following standard body measurement, and **record** them at once. Assessors watch the order and the client's position, not only the numbers.

The standard measurements include the shoulder, neck circumference, chest width and bust circumference, bust height and width, front and back figure, **waistline**, **hips**, **armhole circumference**, and the lengths of the sleeve, blouse, skirt or dress.

Before measuring, the dressmaker plans the design with the client, agreeing on fabric and special needs such as the kind of collar, sleeve, pocket or skirt. Measurements without a clear design waste time.
Memory aid: "Tools ready, client still, same order, write it down."
Sources: SRC-0080 Draft and cut pattern unit, element 2 and range of variables 4–5

title: Clothing care labels
md:
Good clothing care starts with the **care label**, which uses five basic pictures.
- A **tub** means washing. The number inside is the highest safe water temperature in degrees Celsius; American labels use dots instead.
- A **triangle** means bleaching. An empty triangle allows bleach, two slanted lines inside mean no chlorine bleach, and a crossed triangle means **no bleach at all**.
- A **square** means drying. A circle inside the square means tumble drying; dots show the heat.
- An **iron** means pressing. One dot is low heat (about 110 °C), two is medium (about 150 °C), three is high (about 200 °C).
- A **circle** alone means professional cleaning, such as dry cleaning.

An X over any symbol means "do not". So a crossed tub means hand-washing or dry cleaning only, and a crossed iron means do not iron. Reading labels before buying also helps you choose clothes you can maintain.
Memory aid: "Tub, Triangle, Square, Iron, Circle = Wash, Bleach, Dry, Press, Pro."
Sources: SRC-0152 Washing, Bleaching, Drying, Ironing, Professional cleaning

title: Design elements and color schemes in clothing
md:
Clothing design uses the same building blocks as art. The **elements of design** are line, shape, form, color, space, texture and value. In a garment, lines come from seams, pleats and stripes; shape is the silhouette; texture is how the fabric looks and feels; value is how light or dark it is.

**Color** has three properties: **hue** (the color name), **intensity** or chroma (how bright or dull), and **value** (how light or dark).

Common color schemes help in choosing outfits. **Monochromatic** uses tints and shades of one hue, calm and unified. **Analogous** uses neighbors on the color wheel, such as yellow, yellow-green and green. **Complementary** pairs opposites, such as blue and orange, for strong contrast. **Split-complementary** uses a color plus the two beside its opposite. **Triadic** uses three evenly spaced hues, such as red, yellow and blue.
Memory aid: "One hue = mono; neighbors = analogous; opposites = complementary; three apart = triad."
Sources: SRC-0154 Line to Value; SRC-0153 color scheme sections

title: Fabric grain and seam allowance
md:
Woven fabric has three directions. The **straight grain** runs along the warp threads, parallel to the **selvedge**, the finished edge. It stretches the least, so most garments are cut with the straight grain running from top to bottom. The **cross grain** runs across, along the weft, and stretches a little more. The **bias** is any diagonal; at 45° it is called true bias. Fabric is stretchiest and most fluid on the bias, which is why bias-cut skirts drape softly and bias tape bends around curves.

**Seam allowance** is the strip between the cut edge and the stitching line. Home-sewing patterns use about 1/4 to 5/8 inch, with 5/8 inch (1.5 cm) common because it keeps fraying fabric safely inside the seam. Curves such as necklines get narrower allowances.

TESDA requires patterns to be pinned along the grain line and seam allowances marked before cutting.
Memory aid: "Selvedge = straight = steady; Bias = bend."
Sources: SRC-0150 Straight grain, Cross grain, Bias; SRC-0149 lead; SRC-0080 Prepare and cut materials

title: Drafting a block pattern and reading pattern symbols
md:
Pattern work moves from basic to specific. First the dressmaker drafts a **basic or block pattern**, also called a sloper, such as a bodice, skirt or trouser block fitted to the client. Then the block is **manipulated** into the chosen style. Finally the pattern is labeled, filed and cut, **with or without seam allowance**. Changing a finished pattern to other sizes is called grading.

Drafting tools listed by TESDA are tailor's chalk, pattern paper, a ruler with grid, a 45°–90° triangle, a hip curve, a French curve and a pencil. Scissors are the cutting tool.

Patterns may be drafted flat from measurements, or made by **draping** cloth on a dress form.

Learn the symbols: a long **arrow** is the grainline and must lie parallel to the straight grain; **notches** mark matching points and seam allowances; **holes** mark darts, pockets and buttonholes; **double lines** show where to lengthen or shorten.
Memory aid: "Block first, style second, arrow on the grain."
Sources: SRC-0080 Draft and cut pattern unit; SRC-0151 lead, Standard pattern symbols

title: Preparing, cutting, sewing and finishing a garment
md:
After the pattern is ready, TESDA's standard follows a clear order. **Prepare the fabric**: check its quality, faults, width and selvedges, then soak or drip-dry and press it so it will not shrink after sewing. Know fabric properties such as weight, shrinkage, pile and grain. **Lay out and pin** the pattern along the grain line, mark seam allowances, and cut.

**Sew** the garment pieces, watching for puckering, uneven stitches, loose threads and skipped stitches. Sleeves may be puff, tailored or cup style.

**Finish** the garment: attach closures and accents such as zippers, buttons, bias tape, and hooks and eyes; fold, pin and sew hem allowances; then **press** with the right tools and heat. Before release, check for grease or oil spots, puckering, loose threads, missing buttons and uneven stitches. A garment is not finished until these faults are fixed.
Memory aid: "Prep, Pin, Cut, Sew, Close, Hem, Press, Inspect."
Sources: SRC-0080 Prepare and cut materials; Sew casual apparel; Apply finishing touches

title: Darts, gathers, pleats, hems and sewing tools
md:
Several sewing terms describe how flat fabric is shaped to the body. A dart is a fold that tapers to a point, stitched to remove extra fabric and give shape, for example at the bust or waist of a blouse. Gathering pulls a loose line of stitching so the edge bunches into many small, soft, irregular folds, as on a gathered skirt. A pleat is a deliberate fold made by doubling fabric back on itself and fixing it, so it looks neat and structured, unlike gathers. A hem finishes an edge: the edge is folded and sewn so it will not unravel, and it sets the garment's length. Two small tools help: a seam ripper cuts and removes unwanted stitches, and a tracing wheel transfers pattern markings onto fabric.
Memory aid: "Dart = Do-fit, Pleat = Pressed, Gather = Gentle bunch."
Sources: SRC-0258 to SRC-0263, lead sections

title: Ethical and professional practice
md:
TESDA treats work ethics as a competency called **practice career professionalism**. It appears in every TLE trade, from cookery to dressmaking, and has three elements.

1. **Integrate personal objectives with organizational goals.** Pursue personal growth plans that improve your qualifications, keep good working relationships, and show commitment to the organization in your daily duties.
2. **Set and meet work priorities.** Rank competing demands so personal, team and organizational goals are met. Use human, financial and technological resources efficiently, and follow procedures for the **economical use and maintenance** of equipment and facilities.
3. **Maintain professional growth.** Take trainings, accept recognition, and obtain and **renew licenses and certifications**, such as TESDA National Certificates.

So an ethical HE worker is not only honest but also careful with the employer's resources and keeps their skills current.
Memory aid: "Goals, Priorities, Growth."
Sources: SRC-0075 Practice career professionalism unit

title: Sanitation Code rules for food establishments and handlers
md:
The Code on Sanitation (PD 856) sets the basic rules for any place where food or drinks are made, processed, stored, sold or served, including a school canteen.

The **establishment** needs a **sanitary permit** from the local health office, posted where customers can see it. If the owner or occupant changes, the change must be noted within fourteen days.

Each **worker** needs a **health certificate** from the local health authority, given only after a physical and medical examination and the required immunizations. Nobody may be hired in a food establishment without one.

On the job, food handlers wear clean working clothes. The cook wears a prescribed cap, and female staff wear caps or hairnets. Handlers keep good personal hygiene and wash their hands with soap and water, then dry them properly, right before work and after every toilet visit.
Memory aid: "Permit on the wall, certificate in the wallet, cap on the head, soap on the hands."
Sources: SRC-0059 Secs. 14, 15, 19

title: Identifying and preventing hygiene risks in the kitchen
md:
TESDA's Cookery standard teaches workplace hygiene in two steps.
1. **Follow hygiene procedures:** handle food safely, wash hands regularly, store food correctly, wear clean clothing, avoid cross-contamination, handle linen and garbage properly, and clean and sanitize.
2. **Identify and prevent hygiene risks.** Typical risks are poor food handling, storage at the wrong temperature, food left uncovered, poor personal hygiene, vermin, airborne dust, cross-contamination from bad cleaning, and contaminated wastes such as blood. Fix the risks that fall within your own responsibility. **Report** the ones beyond your control to the right person.

Cleaning the kitchen uses chemicals and clean potable water, follows a cleaning schedule, and ends with sorting waste and disposing of chemicals safely. Clean utensils are stacked in their designated place.
Memory aid: "Follow, Find, Fix or Flag."
Sources: SRC-0075 Observe workplace hygiene procedures; Clean and maintain kitchen premises

title: OSH program, committee and safety officer
md:
RA 11058 makes safety an organized system, not a poster on the wall. Every covered workplace needs a written **safety and health program**, made with the workers and submitted to DOLE. It covers things like a drug-free workplace, disease prevention, PPE, signage, toolbox meetings, accident reporting and an emergency plan.

An **OSH committee** watches over the program. The **employer chairs** it, the **safety officer serves as secretary**, and health personnel and **workers' representatives** sit as members. The safety officer, trained by DOLE, monitors and inspects, helps government inspectors, and can **issue work stoppage orders**.

All workers take an **eight-hour safety seminar**. The employer pays for the program as part of operating costs. Willful violations can cost up to **one hundred thousand pesos a day** until fixed, and everyone who manages the work is jointly liable.
Memory aid: "Boss chairs, Officer writes, Workers sit — and the Officer can stop the work."
Sources: SRC-0063 Secs. 12–16, 21, 28

title: Safe, clean and efficient salon work
md:
TESDA's Beauty Care standard has a whole unit on keeping the salon safe, clean and efficient. It has five parts.

First, **comply with health regulations**: follow the salon's personal hygiene rules and local health rules. Second, **check your own work area**: keep reception, stations and walkways clear and organized, dispose of waste properly, and remove spills, hair and other hazards from the floor right away. Linen is stored, cleaned and disinfected. Third, **check tools and equipment**: store them safely, prepare them for each service, and send faulty ones for repair. Fourth, **manage stock**: rotate stock, record levels, report shortages or wrong deliveries, and lift and carry safely. Fifth, **care for clients** so they feel comfortable and are consulted.

Many slips, cuts and infections in salons come from small lapses such as hair on the floor or unclean towels.
Memory aid: "Rules, Room, Tools, Stock, Client."
Sources: SRC-0079 safe, clean and efficient work environment unit

title: Worker duties and work ethics
Baking equipment, dough types and techniques
md:
Baking is precise, so TESDA's standard says ingredients are **selected, measured and weighed** by recipe, and the oven temperature is chosen for the product.

Key equipment: commercial mixers, scales and measures, bowls, cutting tools, ovens, moulds and cutters, baking sheets and pans of different sizes.

Know the dough families. **Lean-yeast dough** gives crisp- and soft-crusted breads, whole-wheat breads and sourdough. **Soft dough** gives loaves and buns. **Rich-yeast dough**, with more fat and sugar, gives sweet dough and laminated (rolled-in) dough. **Quick breads** such as muffins and shortcakes rise without yeast.

Techniques include beating, whisking, folding, rolling, laminating, creaming, kneading and proofing, then scaling, panning and baking. Finished goods are judged by color, texture, moisture, mouth feel and appearance, and stored with attention to temperature, light, air and labels.
Memory aid: "Weigh it, mix it, proof it, bake it, judge it, label it."
Sources: SRC-0076 Prepare and produce bakery products unit

title: Using computer technology in HE work
md:
Every TESDA HE qualification includes the unit "Perform computer operations." It has five elements.
1. **Plan and prepare:** decide what the task needs, choose the right hardware and software, and plan to follow OHS guidelines.
2. **Input data:** enter it with the right program, check it for accuracy, save it, and store it on suitable media.
3. **Access information:** open the right application and navigate with the desktop icons.
4. **Produce output:** process the data, print it, or transfer files between compatible systems.
5. **Maintain the system:** clean the equipment, do minor maintenance, replace consumables, keep **regular back-ups**, run **virus checks**, and maintain files.

All of this is done within **ergonomic guidelines**, with safe keyboard technique. Hardware includes personal computers, networked systems, printers, scanners, keyboards and mice.
Memory aid: "Plan, Put in, Pull up, Print out, Protect."
Sources: SRC-0075 Perform computer operations

title: Choosing cleaning equipment, chemicals and protective clothing
md:
In housekeeping, the surface decides the method. TESDA's unit on cleaning public areas starts with **selecting and setting up** equipment and materials.

Choose equipment for the type of cleaning, and check it is clean and safe before you use it. Choose suitable **dry or wet cleaning agents** according to the manufacturer's directions and safety rules. Wear **protective clothing** when needed, such as aprons, overalls, goggles and masks, waterproof clothing and footwear.

Then match chemicals to the **material**: glass, leather, fabrics, brass or steel, wood, carpet and hard floors each need different products. A glass cleaner is wrong for leather, and a harsh chemical can damage wood.

Stay alert to hazards: spills, wet or slippery floors, fumes, broken glass, sharp objects, hot surfaces, and dangerous waste like blood or used needles, which need special handling.
Memory aid: "Surface first, chemical second, gear on, eyes open."
Sources: SRC-0078 Clean public areas, facilities and equipment unit

title: Kitchen and bakery tools; cooking methods
md:
Cooking starts with **mise en place**. Clean and sanitize the tools, assemble the ingredients by quantity and quality, thaw frozen items properly, and wash raw produce in potable water. TESDA's meat-dish tools include knives, a meat mallet, meat hooks, larding needles, sharpening and honing tools, slicers, a meat thermometer, weighing scales and kitchen twine.

Cooking methods fall into three groups:
- **Dry heat:** roasting, grilling, broiling, baking, pan frying, deep-fat frying.
- **Moist heat:** boiling, steaming, poaching, simmering.
- **Combination:** braising and stewing.

A bakery adds commercial mixers, scales and measures, ovens, moulds and cutters, baking sheets and pans. Ingredients are weighed to the recipe, and the oven temperature suits the product. Baking techniques include creaming, folding, kneading, laminating and proofing.
Memory aid: "Dry bakes, Moist boils, Combo braises."
Sources: SRC-0075 Prepare meat dishes; SRC-0076 Prepare and produce bakery products

title: Cleaning and maintaining kitchen equipment and premises
md:
TESDA's Cookery standard splits kitchen cleaning into three jobs.

1. **Clean, sanitize and store equipment.** Choose the right chemicals and use clean, potable water on utensils, pots, chopping boards and working surfaces. Follow the manufacturer's instructions, then store or stack clean items safely in their designated place. Cleaning equipment itself is assembled, used and stored safely.
2. **Clean and sanitize premises.** Follow the cleaning schedule. Clean walls, floors, shelves, ovens and cold storage without harming people or property. If someone is hurt, follow first aid procedures.
3. **Dispose of waste.** Sort waste according to sanitary rules, and dispose of used cleaning chemicals by standard procedure, never casually.

Supplies include chemical dispensers, paper towels, cleaning agents and sanitizers. Workers should also know eco-friendly cleaning products and how cross-contamination happens.
Memory aid: "Equipment, Premises, Waste — clean, sanitize, store, sort."
Sources: SRC-0075 Clean and maintain kitchen premises unit

title: Measuring, drafting, cutting and pressing tools for sewing
md:
TESDA's Dressmaking standard sorts sewing tools by job.
- **Measuring:** tape measure and meter stick, in either the English or the metric system. Pattern drafting adds the hip curve rule and the L-square.
- **Drafting:** tailor's chalk, pattern paper, a ruler with grid, a 45°–90° triangle, a hip curve, a French curve and a pencil.
- **Cutting:** scissors. Patterns are cut either with or without seam allowance.
- **Pressing:** flat iron, ironing board, sleeve board, press mitt and tailor's ham.
- **Machines:** single-needle and double-needle lockstitch machines, edging machines and buttonhole machines.

On the exam, first decide which stage the task belongs to: measuring, drafting, cutting, sewing or pressing. Then pick a tool from that group. A tailor's ham will never be the answer for drafting, and an L-square will never be the answer for pressing.
Memory aid: "Measure, Draft, Cut, Sew, Press — pick the tool from the right box."
Sources: SRC-0080 measurements; draft and cut pattern; finishing touches; machines

title: Sewing machines, maintenance and measuring tools
md:
A dressmaking shop uses four kinds of machines: the **single-needle lockstitch** machine for ordinary seams, the double-needle lockstitch, the **edging** machine for finishing raw edges, and the **buttonhole** machine.

Basic maintenance has three steps. Start, stop and watch the machine as the manufacturer directs. **Clean and lubricate** it according to the manufacturer's instructions. Check that it runs correctly, and **write down and report** any problem to the supervisor.

TESDA separates faults by seriousness. **Minor faults** such as loose threads, a broken needle or a control problem can usually be fixed by the operator. **Major faults** such as a defective electric motor, timing that is not synchronized, or broken body parts need a technician.

For drafting patterns, the standard measuring tools are the tape measure, hip curve rule, L-square and meter stick.
Memory aid: "Needle broke? Fix it. Motor or timing? Report it."
Sources: SRC-0080 Set up and operate machine; Perform basic maintenance; Draft and cut pattern

title: Conducting competency-based assessment
md:
TESDA trains assessors to run a competency assessment in six steps.
1. **Organize** the assessment: identify activities using the Evidence Guide, prepare resources in a safe setting, and inform the right people.
2. **Prepare the candidate:** explain the purpose, the competency standard, the evidence to be collected and the procedure, and check whether the candidate needs an allowable adjustment.
3. **Gather evidence** using the methods in the Evidence Guide, such as demonstration with oral questioning, written tests or portfolios, and document it with the assessment tools.
4. **Make the decision:** judge the evidence against the rules of evidence and the dimensions of competency. The result is competent or not yet competent.
5. **Record** results accurately and keep them confidential.
6. **Give feedback:** be clear and constructive, explore gaps, and tell the candidate about reassessment.

An HE teacher uses the same steps for a cookery practical.
Memory aid: "Only Prepared Grads Do Real Fieldwork" = Organize, Prepare, Gather, Decide, Record, Feedback.
Sources: SRC-0081 Conduct competency assessment unit

title: Assessment, measurement, evaluation; formative and summative
md:
Three words are often confused. **Assessment** is the whole process of gathering information about learning, from projects, portfolios, performances, observations and tests, and judging progress. **Measurement** answers "how much?" by assigning a number, such as 28 out of 30. **Evaluation** is the judgment made from that information, about a learner, a method or one's own teaching.

**Assessment for learning** is mostly **formative**. It happens during instruction so teachers can change their teaching and learners can improve. It may be **informal**, like noticing errors while students work, or **formal**, like a planned skills checklist.

**Assessment of learning** is mostly **summative**. It comes after instruction to certify mastery, decide readiness for the next unit, and give grades.

The key test for "formative" is use: results feed back into teaching before the unit ends.
Memory aid: "Formative forms the learning; summative sums it up."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Basic concepts

title: Performance, alternative and authentic assessment
md:
In a **performance assessment**, learners carry out a complex task while the teacher judges both the **process** and the **product**. In Home Economics, that might be preparing a meal, sewing a blouse or setting a table. The teacher watches knife handling and sanitation, not only the finished dish.

Two related terms differ. **Alternative assessment** means any task that is not pencil-and-paper. **Authentic assessment** means a task close to what people do in the real world. Authenticity is a matter of degree: running the school canteen for a day is highly authentic; matching cooking terms to definitions is not.

Performance assessments assess complex outcomes, show learners the goal clearly, and usually have strong content validity. Their drawbacks are that they take a lot of time, so fewer can be given, and they are hard to score reliably unless the teacher uses clear rubrics.
Memory aid: "Process + Product; Real world = Authentic; Not paper = Alternative."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Performance assessments; Advantages and disadvantages

title: Portfolio types and purposes
md:
A **portfolio** is a meaningful, purposeful collection of student work that tells the story of achievement or growth. It is not a folder of everything.

Seifert and Sutton describe four pairs of purposes.
- **For learning vs of learning:** for-learning portfolios stress self-reflection and student choice; of-learning portfolios certify achievement, with less choice.
- **Progress vs current accomplishment:** progress portfolios show growth, sometimes with drafts; others show only recent finished work.
- **Showcase vs documentation:** a showcase holds the student's **best work**, chosen with feedback; a documentation portfolio includes **all** samples.
- **Finished vs working:** a finished portfolio is polished for an audience, such as a job application; a **working portfolio** collects day-to-day work and is **not meant for grading**.

In TLE, a cookery portfolio might include recipes, photos, self-assessments and teacher feedback.
Memory aid: "For/Of, Growth/Now, Best/All, Done/Working."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Portfolios

title: PQF and national certification
md:
Competency assessment in TLE connects to national qualifications. The **Philippine Qualifications Framework**, set by **RA 10968 (2018)**, describes levels of educational qualifications and sets standards for their outcomes. Each level is described in terms of **knowledge, skills and values**, **application**, and **degree of independence**. The PQF harmonizes qualification levels across **basic education, technical-vocational education and higher education**, and supports lifelong learning and the **recognition of prior learning**.

Under the **TESDA Act (RA 7796)**, national occupational skills standards are set by TESDA-accredited **industry committees**. TESDA runs certification and accreditation, and accredited industry groups conduct trade tests. Each TESDA training regulation, such as Cookery NC II or Dressmaking NC II, states these standards unit by unit.

So a TLE teacher's classroom assessment should mirror the competency standards that the national assessment will use.
Memory aid: "PQF levels = Know, Apply, Independence; TESDA standards = Industry-set."
Sources: SRC-0042 Secs. 4, 5, 8; SRC-0043 Sec. 22

title: Purposes of assessment and types of evidence
md:
Why assess at all? TESDA's trainer standard lists several purposes. Assessment can **certify** that someone is competent, help **recruit and select** trainees, monitor work performance, find **training needs**, audit skills, **recognize prior learning**, classify a person against industry standards, and give **feedback on progress** during training.

**Recognition of prior learning (RPL)** matters in TLE: a learner who already sews well from helping at a family shop can be assessed and credited without repeating the whole course.

Evidence may be **direct**, such as watching the learner perform, or **indirect**, such as a supervisor's third-party report or a portfolio of past work. Good practice combines methods.

When a trainer prepares assessment instruments, TESDA asks that they be checked for **validity, fairness, safety and cost-effectiveness**, and that the method match the learning outcome of the module.
Memory aid: "Certify, Select, Monitor, Diagnose, Audit, Recognize, Classify, Coach."
Sources: SRC-0081 Conduct competency assessment, range of variables; Plan training session, element 4

title: Holistic and analytic rubrics
md:
A **scoring rubric** describes what performance looks like at each level, so different raters, or the same rater on different days, score more consistently. This improves reliability, which is the weak point of performance tasks.

A **holistic rubric** gives one overall score from general descriptions, such as not proficient, partially proficient, proficient and advanced. It is quicker to build and to use, and suits a final overall judgment.

An **analytic rubric** describes levels for each criterion separately. For a sewing project the criteria might be measurement accuracy, seam quality, finishing, pressing and workplace safety, each scored on its own. It takes longer to build, but it shows learners exactly what to improve, so it is better for formative feedback.

Whichever type you choose, share the rubric with learners before the task.
Memory aid: "Holistic = one big score; Analytic = one score per part."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Scoring rubrics

title: Action research cycle
md:
**Action research**, a term coined by **Kurt Lewin** in 1944, is research by teachers on their own students or their own teaching, aimed at concrete improvements. Lewin described it as a spiral of steps, each a circle of planning, action and fact-finding.

Seifert and Sutton, following Mertler, describe four stages.
1. **Planning:** identify and define the problem as a researchable question, review related literature, and plan what data to collect, how and when.
2. **Acting:** collect and analyze data. Keep it simple and manageable.
3. **Developing an action plan:** make changes in teaching and document them.
4. **Communicating and reflecting:** share results with colleagues, then ask "What did I learn? What should I do next?" This starts a new cycle.

Example: an HE teacher notices poor handwashing in the kitchen lab, tries a visual checklist, observes compliance for three weeks, and shares results at a faculty meeting.
Memory aid: "Plan, Act, Change, Share and Reflect — then spiral again."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 1, Ch. 11 Cycles of planning, acting and reflecting; SRC-0169 lead

title: Variables, control groups and blinding
md:
An experiment tests whether changing one thing causes a change in another. The variable the researcher changes is the **explanatory variable**, also called the independent variable. The variable measured is the **response variable**, or dependent variable. For example, if a teacher compares two ways of teaching knife skills, the teaching method is explanatory and the skills score is the response.

Other factors can cloud the result; these are **lurking variables**, such as prior cooking experience at home. Good design isolates the explanatory variable, usually by **random assignment** to groups.

A **control group** gets no treatment or the usual treatment, so the effect of simply being studied is balanced out. **Blinding** keeps participants from knowing which treatment they got, which counters the power of suggestion. In a **double-blind** study, neither the participants nor the researchers working with them know.
Memory aid: "Explain → Response; Control the rest; Blind the bias."
Sources: SRC-0091 1.4

title: Parts of a research paper (IMRaD)
md:
Most research articles follow **IMRaD**: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion.
- **Introduction:** Why was the study done? What is the research question or hypothesis?
- **Methods:** Who took part, when, where and how was the study done, and with what materials or instruments?
- **Results:** What did the study find? Was the hypothesis supported?
- **Discussion:** What do the findings mean, how do they fit other research, and what should be studied next?

The flow is often drawn as a **wine glass** or hourglass: wide and general at the start, narrow and specific in the methods and results, then wide again in the discussion.

A quick test: a sentence describing the sample and instrument belongs in Methods; a percentage or mean belongs in Results; "this suggests" belongs in Discussion. Papers may also carry funding and ethics statements.
Memory aid: "I Must Report Discoveries" = Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion.
Sources: SRC-0168 lead, Overview, Other elements

title: Population, sample, parameter, statistic; types of data
md:
Suppose an HE teacher wants to know how much Grade 8 learners in a division spend on snacks each week. All Grade 8 learners in the division are the **population**. The 120 learners actually surveyed are the **sample**.

A number describing the population, such as the true average spending, is a **parameter**. The same number computed from the sample is a **statistic**. We use statistics to estimate parameters.

Data come in two kinds. **Qualitative** or categorical data describe attributes in words or labels, such as favorite snack or barangay. They are shown with pie charts and bar graphs. **Quantitative** data are numbers from counting or measuring, such as pesos spent or number of snacks. Quantitative data may be **discrete**, from counting, or **continuous**, from measuring.
Memory aid: "Sample–Statistic, Population–Parameter; Qualitative = Quality words, Quantitative = Quantity numbers."
Sources: SRC-0091 1.1, 1.2

title: Ethics in classroom research
md:
Teachers routinely collect test scores and observations to teach. Research adds ethical duties. If action-research data will be shared **outside the school community**, for example at a conference or in a journal, the teacher must obtain permission from **parents or guardians and the students**.

This is usually done with an **informed consent form**. It summarizes the study, describes the data to be collected, states that participation is **voluntary**, and promises **confidentiality or anonymity**. Unlike regular class tasks, students may decline to take part in the research.

Statistics texts likewise require informed consent from all participants. In the Philippines, the Data Privacy Act treats learners' education and health information as **sensitive personal information**, so research data must be protected and reported without identifying individual learners.
Memory aid: "Inform, Ask, Allow refusal, Anonymize."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Ethical issues; SRC-0091 1.4; SRC-0045 Sec. 3(l)

title: Sampling methods
md:
How a sample is chosen decides whether results can be trusted. OpenStax describes four random methods and one common non-random one.
- **Simple random sample:** every member has an equal chance, like drawing names from a box.
- **Stratified sample:** split the population into groups called strata, such as grade levels, then take a proportionate random sample from **each** group.
- **Cluster sample:** split the population into clusters, such as sections, then randomly choose **some whole clusters** and include everyone in them.
- **Systematic sample:** pick a random starting point, then take **every nth** person from a list.
- **Convenience sample:** use whoever is easy to reach, such as the first learners who arrive at the canteen. It is not random and can be badly biased.

For a canteen survey, stratifying by grade level makes sure every grade is represented.
Memory aid: "Strata = Some from every group; Cluster = Choose whole groups; Systematic = every nth."
Sources: SRC-0091 1.2

title: Act No. 74 (1901) and the American public school system
md:
The Philippine public school system as a national, government-run system traces back to Act No. 74 of 1901, passed by the Philippine Commission during the American period. The act did several things.
- It created a Department of Public Instruction for the Philippine Islands, with its central office in Manila.
- It brought the schools set up under the military government under that department.
- It made all primary instruction in its schools free.
- It ordered that English be made the basis of all public school instruction as soon as practicable.
- It allowed soldiers to serve as teachers until trained teachers could replace them.

The act also funded a normal school, meaning a school for training teachers, and a trade school in Manila, and an agricultural school. When an exam asks which law established the public school system in the American period, or made English the medium, the answer is Act No. 74.
Memory aid: "Act 74 — free, public, English."
Sources: SRC-0011 Secs. 1, 2, 14 and title

title: Conflict theory, symbolic interactionism, feminist theory of education
md:
Not every sociologist sees schools as neutral.
- **Conflict theorists** argue that education can widen social inequality. One mechanism is the hidden curriculum: nonacademic lessons learned through informal learning and cultural transmission, which reward students who already have more cultural capital. Another is tracking, which sorts students into advanced and low groups. Conflict theorists say tracking keeps inequality in place and creates self-fulfilling prophecies.
- **Symbolic interactionists** look at everyday interaction between teachers and students. When a student is labeled a low achiever, the label is hard to shake off and can come true because people act on it.
- **Feminist theorists** study how gender inequality is rooted in, and repeated by, education.

For teachers, the practical lesson is to watch what expectations, groupings and labels communicate, not only what the official lesson plan says.
Memory aid: "Conflict counts winners; interaction watches labels."
Sources: SRC-0088 section 16.2

title: 1987 Constitution, Article XIV on education
Functionalism — manifest and latent functions of education
md:
Functionalists see education as one of society's most important institutions, doing two kinds of work. Manifest, or primary, functions are the intended and visible ones. The first is socialization. The French sociologist Émile Durkheim called schools socialization agencies that teach children to get along with others and prepare them for adult economic roles. Another manifest function is social control: schools teach students to follow rules, obey laws and respect authority, which prepares them for the workplace. Latent, or secondary, functions are hidden and unintended by-products of going to school. Examples include meeting a future partner, building friendships and networks that later help in finding a job, and learning to work in small groups. On the exam, decide whether the outcome was the school's purpose. If it was, it is a manifest function; if it was a side effect, it is latent.
Memory aid: "Manifest = meant; latent = by-product."
Sources: SRC-0088 section 16.2

title: Inclusive education under RA 11650
md:
Republic Act 11650 of 2022 makes inclusion the policy of every early and basic education school, public and private. No learner may be denied admission because of a disability. The law defines inclusive education as responding to the diverse needs of all learners so that they can fully participate, be present and achieve. This involves accommodation, modification, adaptation and individualization of content, approaches, structures and strategies. Each learner with a disability may have an Individualized Education Plan. The IEP sets out the learner's present level, the services to be provided, and their duration and frequency. DepEd and local governments must set up at least one Inclusive Learning Resource Center in every city and municipality, and all existing SPED Centers are renamed as such centers. The centers run the Child Find System, which identifies, locates and evaluates learners with disabilities who are out of school, so they can be included.
Memory aid: "Find them (Child Find), plan for them (IEP), support them (ILRC)."
Sources: SRC-0032 Secs. 3–7

title: RA 10627 Anti-Bullying Act
md:
The Anti-Bullying Act of 2013 (RA 10627) defines bullying as severe or repeated use, by one or more students, of written, verbal or electronic expression, or a physical act or gesture, against another student. To count, it must cause fear of harm, create a hostile school environment, infringe the victim's rights, or disrupt schooling. Every elementary and secondary school, public or private, must adopt an anti-bullying policy. The policy covers bullying on school grounds, at school activities, on school vehicles and through school technology, and also forbids retaliation against people who report. The principal oversees the policy. Staff, students, parents and volunteers must report bullying they witness. Schools report their policies, and later yearly bullying statistics, to the schools division superintendent. Note that the law's definition is about students bullying students.
Memory aid: "Student to student, school must have a policy."
Sources: SRC-0025 Secs. 2–5

title: RA 4670 benefits and freedom to organize
md:
Beyond workload and job security, RA 4670 lists several benefits.
- Teachers get a compulsory, free medical examination before they start teaching and at least once a year after that.
- Physical and nervous strain is recognized as a compensable occupational disease.
- After seven years of service, a teacher may take a study leave of up to one school year at no less than sixty percent of monthly salary.
- An indefinite sick leave is allowed when treatment will last more than a year.
- On retirement, the teacher receives a one-range salary raise that becomes the basis of retirement pay.
- No one may deduct from a teacher's salary unless the law allows it, although association dues and insurance premiums may be deducted with written consent.
- Teachers may form and join organizations freely, without prior permission. Punishing a teacher for membership is unlawful discrimination.
Memory aid: "7-1-60" — 7 years of service, 1 school year of leave, 60 percent pay.
Sources: SRC-0019 Secs. 21–28

title: RA 7610 and RA 9262 child and family protection
md:
Two laws help a teacher recognize abuse.
- **RA 7610** gives special protection to children, meaning persons below eighteen and older persons who cannot protect themselves because of a disability or condition. Child abuse includes physical and psychological abuse, neglect, cruelty, sexual abuse and emotional maltreatment. It also includes acts or words that debase or demean a child's dignity, and unreasonable deprivation of basic needs.
- **RA 9262**, the Anti-VAWC law, covers violence against a woman by her husband, former husband, or a man she has or had a sexual or dating relationship or a child with. It also covers violence against her child. The harm can be physical, sexual, psychological, or economic abuse, such as controlling or withholding financial support.

A learner's home situation may show signs of either. The teacher's role is to recognize the signs and report through proper school channels, not to investigate alone.
Memory aid: "Under 18 = RA 7610; mother and child at home = RA 9262."
Sources: SRC-0029 Sec. 3; SRC-0028 Sec. 3

title: RA 10912 Continuing Professional Development
md:
Passing the LET is a beginning, not an end. The Continuing Professional Development Act of 2016 (RA 10912) makes CPD a mandatory requirement for renewing the professional identification card of every professional regulated by the PRC, teachers included. CPD programs aim to upgrade professionals' competencies and qualifications in line with the Philippine Qualifications Framework, the ASEAN Qualifications Reference Framework, and ASEAN mutual recognition arrangements. In short, CPD keeps a license current and supports career progression and specialization. RA 7836 adds an older idea of growth: teachers may take an oral and written merit examination at least once every five years, free of charge, as an extra basis for merit promotion. Keep the two apart in your head. CPD is tied to renewing the professional ID. The merit exam is optional and is used for promotion.
Memory aid: "CPD renews the ID; the merit exam promotes."
Sources: SRC-0030 Secs. 4, 10; SRC-0016 Sec. 19

title: RA 7836 licensure and the Board for Professional Teachers
md:
RA 7836, the Philippine Teachers Professionalization Act of 1994, makes teaching a licensed profession. Nobody may practice as a professional teacher without a certificate of registration and a professional license from the PRC, unless the law allows a special or temporary permit. The law created the Board for Professional Teachers. It has five members appointed by the President and serving three-year terms, and no one may serve more than two consecutive terms. The Board fixes exam dates, issues and revokes certificates, and adopts a code of ethical standards. The LET must be given at least once a year. For secondary teachers it has three parts: general education, professional education and the field of specialization. Every new registrant takes a professional oath before practicing, and a name enters the roster of professional teachers on registration.
Memory aid: "License before lesson" — no license, no classroom (Sec. 27).
Sources: SRC-0016 Secs. 5–7, 13–14, 17–18, 27

title: RA 9293 eligibility (18 units, 12-unit refresher)
md:
RA 9293 (2004) amended RA 7836. Under the original law, a graduate of arts and sciences needed only ten units of professional education to take the LET. RA 9293 raised this to eighteen units. It also covered teachers of vocational and two-year technical courses: they need a bachelor's degree in their field plus at least eighteen units of professional education. A second change concerns teachers who stop practicing. A registered teacher who has not taught for five years must complete at least twelve units of education courses before returning to the classroom. So if a question describes a nursing or engineering graduate who earned education units to become eligible, the law at work is RA 9293, not the original RA 7836 and never RA 4670.
Memory aid: "18 to enter, 12 to re-enter" (after 5 idle years).
Sources: SRC-0017 Secs. 1–2; SRC-0016 Sec. 15

title: RA 7877 and RA 11313 harassment in schools
md:
The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act (RA 7877) covers work, education and training settings. In a school, the offender is a teacher, instructor, professor, coach or trainer who has authority, influence or moral ascendancy over the student. That person commits sexual harassment by demanding, requesting or otherwise requiring a sexual favor, whether or not the student gives in. The act needs no physical contact, and no acceptance by the student. The Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313) widened protection against gender-based sexual harassment. Every school, public or private, must designate an officer to receive complaints and must adopt and publish grievance procedures. School heads must post a copy of the law, run prevention campaigns, and set up an independent body to investigate complaints. School heads may themselves be liable if they fail to act.
Memory aid: "Power plus a demand equals harassment — the answer does not matter."
Sources: SRC-0026 Sec. 3; SRC-0027 Secs. 21–23

title: RA 4670 teaching hours and extra pay
md:
The Magna Carta for Public School Teachers (RA 4670) limits actual classroom teaching to six hours a day. The schedule should leave the teacher time to prepare lessons and check students' work. When the needs of the service demand it, a teacher may be asked to teach longer, but never more than eight hours a day. Those extra hours must be paid at the regular rate plus at least twenty-five percent of basic pay. A separate rule covers duties beyond normal teaching, such as co-curricular and out-of-school activities. If they are done after six hours of classroom teaching, the teacher earns additional pay of at least twenty-five percent. Exam traps often swap six and eight, or claim that eight hours is the normal load. Remember that the cap applies to actual classroom teaching time, not to all school-related work.
Memory aid: "6 is the rule, 8 is the roof, 25 is the reward."
Sources: SRC-0019 Secs. 13–14

title: RA 4670 tenure, transfer and disciplinary safeguards
md:
RA 4670 protects a public school teacher's job. Security of tenure is assured. A teacher hired on provisional status for lack of civil service eligibility serves a probation of at least one year, and becomes permanent after at least ten years of continuous, efficient and faithful service. A teacher cannot be transferred without consent except for cause. When the service requires a transfer, the superintendent must first explain the reasons, and the teacher may appeal. If charges are filed, the teacher has the right to be informed in writing, to see all the evidence, to defend themselves with a representative of their choice, and to appeal. The case must not be publicized while pending. The first hearing is held by a committee chaired by the Schools Division Superintendent, with a teachers' organization representative and a division supervisor.
Memory aid: "WEDA" — Written charges, Evidence access, Defense, Appeal.
Sources: SRC-0019 Secs. 4–6, 8–9

title: Understanding by Design (backward design)
md:
**Understanding by Design (UbD)**, by Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe (1998), is a **backward design** approach. Its authors noticed that teachers often begin planning with a favorite activity or the next textbook chapter. UbD reverses that.

**Stage 1: Identify desired results.** What should students understand and be able to do? Write "Students will understand that…" statements and essential questions, drawing on content standards.

**Stage 2: Determine acceptable evidence.** Decide how students will show that understanding, usually through performance tasks and other assessments.

**Stage 3: Plan learning experiences.** Only now choose the activities and materials that will lead students to the results and prepare them for the assessment.

The key difference from many models is that **assessment is planned before activities**. In an HE unit on meal planning, the teacher first defines the understanding, then designs a family-menu task, then plans lessons.
Memory aid: "Results, Evidence, Activities — begin with the end."
Sources: SRC-0178 lead, Backward design

title: Bloom's taxonomy, original and revised
md:
**Bloom's taxonomy** classifies educational objectives. It was developed by a committee chaired by **Benjamin Bloom** in **1956** and covers three domains: **cognitive** (thinking), **affective** (feelings and values) and **psychomotor** (physical skills).

The original cognitive domain had six levels: Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Analysis, Synthesis and Evaluation. The **2001 revision** renamed them as verbs and swapped the top two: **Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create**. So in the revision, Create is the highest level.

The affective handbook came out in 1964. Bloom's group did not finish the psychomotor domain; **Elizabeth Simpson** later proposed a seven-level psychomotor taxonomy.

The LET table of specifications itself uses the revised levels, so you should be able to tell, for example, that "design a weekly menu" is Create while "judge which menu is healthier" is Evaluate.
Memory aid: "Real Understanding Always Achieves Excellent Creations."
Sources: SRC-0179 lead, History, Cognitive, Psychomotor

title: Hidden curriculum
md:
Not everything students learn in school is in the curriculum guide. The **hidden curriculum** is the set of lessons "which are learned but not openly intended" to be taught: the norms, values and beliefs that come through classroom routines and the school's social life.

Examples include learning to wait your turn, learning who gets called on most, learning that some groups are seated in front, or learning ideas about gender from which students are asked to carry chairs and which to clean. During breaks, students learn unspoken lessons about cliques, bullying, self-expression and conflict resolution.

The hidden curriculum can reinforce existing social inequalities even when the school aims for equal development. Learners with limited social awareness, such as some learners with autism, may miss these unwritten norms unless they are taught directly.

Teachers should notice what their routines teach without words.
Memory aid: "Hidden = learned but never planned."
Sources: SRC-0181 lead

title: K to 12 structure and curriculum standards (RA 10533)
md:
The **Enhanced Basic Education Act (RA 10533, 2013)** set up K to 12: at least **one year of kindergarten**, **six years of elementary**, and **six years of secondary**, made up of **four years of junior high** and **two years of senior high**. Kindergarten entrants are at least five; typical entry ages are six for Grade 1, twelve for junior high and sixteen for senior high.

**DepEd** designs the curriculum, coordinating with **CHED** and **TESDA** and consulting other stakeholders. Section 5 lists the standards the curriculum must meet. It must be learner-centered, inclusive and developmentally appropriate; relevant, responsive and research-based; culture-sensitive; contextualized and global; taught through constructivist, inquiry-based, reflective, collaborative and integrative approaches; built on **spiral progression**; and **flexible**, so schools can localize, indigenize and enhance it. A Curriculum Consultative Committee chaired by the DepEd Secretary reviews it.
Memory aid: "K + 6 + 4 + 2; learner-centered, spiral, flexible to localize."
Sources: SRC-0021 Secs. 4–6

title: Medium of instruction after RA 12027
md:
Under RA 10533 (2013), kindergarten and Grades 1 to 3 were taught in the learners' **mother tongue**, following Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE), which moves "from the known to the unknown".

That changed in **2024**. **RA 12027** **discontinued** the use of the mother tongue as the medium of instruction from kindergarten to Grade 3. Instruction reverts to **Filipino and English**, as the Constitution provides, and **regional languages serve as auxiliary media** of instruction.

MTB-MLE has not vanished completely. It may still be used in **monolingual classes**, meaning classes whose learners share the same mother tongue, if requirements are met: an official KWF orthography, documented vocabulary, reading materials, a grammar book, and trained teachers. DepEd and KWF must develop a **language mapping** policy.

Many older reviewers still describe MTB-MLE as current. On the LET, answer with RA 12027.
Memory aid: "2024: Mother tongue out as medium; Filipino and English in; MTB only in monolingual classes."
Sources: SRC-0022 Secs. 1–2; SRC-0021 Sec. 5(f)

title: Writing learning objectives (Mager and Gronlund)
md:
There are two ways to write objectives. The **cognitive approach** (Gronlund) starts **general**: state a broad goal, such as "understand photosynthesis", then list a few representative **indicators** of success. The list cannot be complete, only representative.

The **behavioral approach** (Mager) starts **specific**. A good behavioral objective has three parts.
1. An **observable behavior**: what the learner will do, such as "list", "measure" or "sew", not "know" or "appreciate".
2. The **conditions**: the circumstances or materials given, such as "given a recipe for four servings".
3. The **criterion**: the minimum acceptable level, such as "with 100 percent accuracy within 15 minutes".

Example: "Given a recipe for four, the learner will scale every ingredient for twelve servings with no errors." Objectives always describe what **students** do, not what the teacher does.
Memory aid: "Behavior, Condition, Degree — can I see it, under what, how well?"
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 10 Formulating learning objectives; behavioral objectives

title: Spiral curriculum
md:
**Jerome Bruner** proposed the **spiral curriculum**: each subject or skill is revisited at intervals, at a **more sophisticated level** each time. Learners first meet the basic ideas, then return to them with more detail, and each return builds on and reinforces what came before. Harden and Stamper add that later encounters should be linked to earlier ones and should increase the learner's competence.

The spiral is not simple repetition. A Grade 7 learner might study basic food groups, a Grade 8 learner the nutrients behind them, and a Grade 10 learner planning balanced meals for a family budget. The topic is the same; the depth grows.

In the Philippines, this is a legal requirement. RA 10533 says the K to 12 curriculum shall use the **spiral progression approach** to ensure mastery of knowledge and skills after each level.
Memory aid: "Same topic, higher turn — like climbing a spiral staircase."
Sources: SRC-0180 lead; SRC-0021 Sec. 5(g)

title: Standards, curriculum frameworks and curriculum guides
md:
Curriculum documents range from broad to detailed. **Standards** state, in general terms, what students should know and be able to do in a subject and grade. They are a first step from big educational purposes toward classroom teaching, but they say little about daily lessons.

A **curriculum framework** organizes the standards for a subject across grade levels. It breaks each standard into a dozen or more specific skills, describes the **scope and sequence**, and names **observable behaviors** that show learning. Sometimes it suggests how to assess them.

A **curriculum guide** is more detailed still, closer to what teachers actually plan from. Even so, teachers must turn guides into unit plans and **objectives** for their own learners.

A quick check on the exam: if a document lists skills by grade without daily activities, it is a framework, not a lesson plan.
Memory aid: "Standards say what; frameworks say in what order; guides say how; teachers say today."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 10 National and state learning standards; Curriculum frameworks and curriculum guides

title: Tyler's model of curriculum development
md:
**Ralph Tyler**, often called the father of educational evaluation, set out a simple model in *Basic Principles of Curriculum and Instruction* (1949). It asks four questions in order.
1. **What educational purposes** should the school seek to attain? This means defining objectives.
2. **What learning experiences** are likely to help attain them? This means selecting experiences.
3. **How should those experiences be organized** for effective instruction?
4. **How can their effectiveness be evaluated?** Evaluate, then revise what did not work.

Tyler stressed the learner's activity: "It is what he does that he learns, not what the teacher does." His ideas grew from his work as head of evaluation for the Eight-Year Study of American high schools in the 1930s.

On the LET, a question that starts from objectives and ends with evaluation is describing Tyler's rationale.
Memory aid: "POOE — Purposes, Opportunities for learning, Organization, Evaluation."
Sources: SRC-0177 Eight-Year Study; Thoughts on curriculum

title: Lectures, advance organizers and concept maps
md:
Lectures and readings are the classic teacher-directed methods. They work only if learners actively listen or read, so teachers add supports.

An **advance organizer**, an idea from **David Ausubel**, is a brief overview given **before** new material, either spoken or drawn. It partly organizes the content for learners so they know where new ideas will fit. For example, before a lesson on food preservation, the teacher shows a chart with three branches: heat, cold and drying, and says the lesson will fill in each branch.

Learners can also organize material themselves. **Outlining** and **note-taking** pull out key points. A **concept map** is a diagram of how concepts relate, usually drawn by the learner; two people's maps of the same idea can reveal how differently they think about it.

The order matters: organizer first, details second.
Memory aid: "Organize in Advance — Ausubel's map before the trip."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 9 Lectures and readings; Advance organizers; Concept maps

title: Choosing and sequencing strategies
md:
No single strategy is best. Seifert and Sutton group strategies along two lines: how much the **teacher directs** the learning, and whether the focus is on **groups or individuals**. Teacher-directed methods include lectures, advance organizers, mastery learning, direct instruction and Hunter's model. Student-centered methods include independent study, inquiry, cooperative learning and projects.

Choose by asking three questions. What kind of **thinking** do I want? How much must the **content be organized** for learners before they can understand it? How much **responsibility** can these learners take for directing their own learning? New, tightly sequenced skills often suit direct instruction; open questions suit inquiry or projects.

Sequence lessons the way the K to 12 law expects: **spiral progression**, from the **known to the unknown**, using constructivist, inquiry-based, reflective, collaborative and integrative approaches.
Memory aid: "Thinking, Organizing, Responsibility — then spiral from known to new."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 9 Table 24, Instructional strategies: an abundance of choices; SRC-0021 Sec. 5

title: Financial, ecological and social literacy
md:
The new literacies stretch "literacy" beyond reading and writing.

**Financial literacy** is the set of skills, knowledge, behaviors and attitudes that let a person make **informed decisions about money**. People with financial training tend to make better choices about budgeting, saving and borrowing. In HE classes, a family budget project builds it directly.

**Ecological literacy**, or ecoliteracy, is understanding the natural systems that make life on Earth possible and using ecological principles to build **sustainable communities**. Educator **David Orr** and physicist **Fritjof Capra** developed the idea in the 1990s. Waste segregation and school gardens are classroom examples.

**Social literacy**, from a sociocultural view, is literacy learned through **social interaction** with peers and adults. Books, games, conversations, field trips and stories, shared between school, family and community, all build it.
Memory aid: "Money sense, Earth sense, People sense."
Sources: SRC-0183 lead; SRC-0185 lead; SRC-0187 lead

title: Madeline Hunter's effective teaching model
md:
**Madeline Hunter** combined several direct-instruction ideas into one lesson model, called **mastery teaching** or the effective teaching model. It has four parts.
1. **Prepare students to learn.** Use the first minutes, when attention is highest. Point ahead with an advance organizer and state the objective clearly.
2. **Present information clearly and explicitly.** Keep one structure, use familiar words and examples, and be concise.
3. **Check for understanding and give guided practice.** Ask questions everyone answers, for example by raising hands, invite choral responses, and sample individuals.
4. **Provide for independent practice.** Do the first few items together, keep solo practice short, and mix in discussion and feedback.

The model needs content broken into small, clear parts. Do not confuse Hunter's **mastery teaching** with **mastery learning**, which is about everyone reaching the same standard with extra time.
Memory aid: "Prepare, Present, Check, Practice."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 9 Madeline Hunter's effective teaching model, Table 25

title: Inquiry and cooperative learning
md:
**Inquiry learning**, also called discovery learning (Bruner) or progressive education (Dewey), turns lecture upside down. The teacher, or sometimes a student, poses a thoughtful question, such as "Why does bread go moldy faster in some kitchens?" The teacher **avoids answering directly**, building on students' ideas with more questions and guiding their investigation. Learners gain new knowledge and practice a way of learning they can reuse.

**Cooperative learning**, or collaborative learning, has students work in groups that are rewarded partly or wholly for **group success**. It needs time and space for talk, and a grading plan. If one grade goes to the whole group, some members may **freeload**. If grades go only to individual parts, members may **overspecialize** and stop cooperating. Good designs combine group goals with individual accountability, and teachers monitor groups and point out quieter members' contributions.
Memory aid: "Inquiry: ask, don't tell. Cooperative: sink or swim together, but each one swims."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 9 Inquiry learning; Cooperative learning

title: Jigsaw, STAD and project-based learning
md:
Three cooperative formats appear often on the LET.

**Jigsaw** (Aronson; Slavin): each member of a home group takes one part of a topic, meets with members of other groups who took the same part to become an **expert**, then returns to **teach** the home group. In a nutrition lesson, one learner becomes the expert on carbohydrates, another on proteins, another on fats.

**STAD**, Student Teams–Achievement Divisions (Slavin): the teacher presents a lesson, teams of four or five study together, and each learner takes a test alone. Scores count partly by **improvement**, so every member helps teammates improve.

**Project-based learning** (Katz): a question or problem of interest is investigated by students working together over an **extended period**, ending in a **product**, presentation or written report, such as a family meal plan with costing.
Memory aid: "Jigsaw = experts teach back; STAD = team improvement points; Project = long work, final product."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 9 Table 26; Ch. 6 jigsaw passage

title: Mastery learning and direct instruction
md:
**Mastery learning** aims for **all learners to reach the same high level**, accepting that some need more time. A typical cycle: a short lesson, then an **ungraded** check. Learners who have mastered it get **enrichment**; others get **tutoring** or extra materials until they master it, then take another test. Two challenges are fairness, since slower learners may get only dull drills, and the need for a detailed curriculum broken into small units.

**Direct instruction** usually means a **highly scripted** form of mastery learning. It mixes behaviorism, such as immediate and explicit praise for correct answers, with cognitive ideas, such as stating objectives in advance and frequent review. Content comes in small, logical steps with lots of practice. Research finds it very effective for **basic skills** such as early reading and arithmetic, especially from kindergarten to Grade 3.
Memory aid: "Mastery = same goal, different time; Direct = small steps, scripted, praised."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 9 Mastery learning; Direct instruction

title: Media and digital literacy
md:
**Media literacy** is the ability to **access, analyze, evaluate and create** media in many forms, and to reflect critically and act ethically. A media-literate learner asks who made a message, why, how it tries to persuade, and what is left out, and can also make responsible media of their own. It can start in early childhood with simple critical-thinking questions about ads.

**Digital literacy** is the ability to **find, evaluate and communicate** information using digital devices and platforms, and to create and share in digital environments. It combines technical skills with thinking skills. The term was first defined by **Paul Gilster in 1997**.

Access alone is not enough. **Henry Jenkins** described a **participation gap**: even where nearly everyone is online, some learners lack the skills and confidence to take part fully. Teachers close it by teaching evaluation and creation, not just clicking.
Memory aid: "Access, Analyze, Evaluate, Create, Act."
Sources: SRC-0182 lead, goals paragraph; SRC-0184 lead, History, Participation gap

title: Multicultural education (Banks)
md:
**Multicultural education** is a set of strategies that teach students about the histories, cultures and contributions of diverse groups, and promote inclusion, diversity and democracy. **James Banks** describes five dimensions teachers should work on.
1. **Content integration:** using examples and content from many cultures.
2. **Knowledge construction:** helping students see how cultural assumptions and biases shape what a field counts as knowledge.
3. **Prejudice reduction:** using methods and materials that change students' attitudes toward other groups.
4. **Equity pedagogy:** changing teaching methods so students from diverse racial, cultural, gender and social-class groups can achieve.
5. **Empowering school culture:** examining grouping, labeling, sports and staff–student interaction so the whole school empowers every learner.

In a Philippine class, featuring Maranao, Ilocano and T'boli dishes in a cookery unit is content integration; adjusting instruction for IP learners is equity pedagogy.
Memory aid: "Content, Knowledge, Prejudice, Equity, Empowering culture."
Sources: SRC-0186 lead, Implementation

title: Natural and logical consequences
md:
When a learner misbehaves, the most effective consequences are closely tied to the behavior itself.

A **natural consequence** happens on its own, without anyone deciding it. A learner who comes late misses the instructions and struggles with the task. A learner who rushes through cooking burns the food.

A **logical consequence** is decided by someone else, such as the teacher, but has an obvious link to the act. A learner who steals a classmate's lunch pays for it. A learner who leaves the kitchen station dirty cleans it before the next activity. A learner who misses class work because of chatting makes it up later as homework.

In real life the two often mix: in a fight, injury may be natural, losing friends logical. Research finds both can reduce misbehavior because learners can see why the consequence follows. Unrelated punishments, such as extra math for talking, teach less.
Memory aid: "Nature happens; Logic is given, but it fits."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 7 Natural and logical consequences

title: Dale's Cone of Experience and choosing media
md:
**Edgar Dale**, an American educator, introduced the **Cone of Experience** in a 1946 textbook on audiovisual teaching and revised it in 1954 and 1969. The cone arranges kinds of learning experiences from the most **concrete** at the base, such as direct, hands-on experience, to the most **abstract** at the tip, such as words and symbols. Its message: young or new learners often need concrete experiences before abstract ones, and media should be chosen with that in mind.

A popular version adds percentages, such as "we remember 10 percent of what we read and 90 percent of what we do". **Dale never included those numbers** and warned readers not to take the cone too literally; the figures came from a later, non-scholarly article. If an item attributes the percentages to Dale, it is wrong.

Choosing media also follows **TPACK**: the medium should fit both the content and the teaching method.
Memory aid: "Concrete at the base, abstract at the tip — and no percentages from Dale."
Sources: SRC-0148 Cone of Experience; SRC-0144 lead

title: Gordon's conflict resolution, I-messages and assertive discipline
md:
For conflicts that need more than a look, Seifert and Sutton describe four steps based on Thomas Gordon's **Teacher Effectiveness Training**.
1. **Decide problem ownership.** The owner is the person primarily troubled by the behavior: the learner, the teacher or a classmate. The owner takes main responsibility for solving it.
2. **Listen actively.** Attend to everything the learner says and keep checking your understanding with questions.
3. **Be assertive and use I-messages.** Speak firmly, neither apologetic nor hostile, as in Canter's assertive discipline. An **I-message** describes how the behavior affects you: "Your talking makes it hard for me to remember what I'm saying." A you-message blames: "You're so rude."
4. **Negotiate** when a problem persists: define it together, brainstorm solutions with the learner, pick one, try it and review.

Dictating a solution to a long-running conflict often leaves everyone feeling defeated.
Memory aid: "O-L-I-N: Ownership, Listen, I-message, Negotiate."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 7 Conflict resolution steps 1–4

title: Education rights of indigenous peoples (IPRA)
md:
The **Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act (RA 8371, 1997)** sets out how the State must educate indigenous cultural communities and indigenous peoples (ICCs/IPs).

Section 28 says the State, through the **National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP)**, shall provide a complete, adequate and **integrated system of education relevant to the needs** of IP children and youth. Section 29 obliges the State to respect and protect IPs' right to **preserve their culture, traditions and institutions**, and to consider these in national plans.

Section 30 gives IPs **equal access** to educational and cultural opportunities **without losing their right** to set up and control their own education systems, **in their own language**, and in ways **appropriate to their cultural methods of teaching and learning**. IP children have the right to all levels and forms of State education.

For a teacher, this means using IP learners' language and community knowledge as resources, not obstacles.
Memory aid: "Relevant, Respectful, in their own Language and ways — Secs. 28, 29, 30."
Sources: SRC-0036 Secs. 28–30

title: Responding to minor misbehavior
md:
Responses to misbehavior should match its size. Seifert and Sutton start with the mildest.

**Ignoring** can be wise when a behavior is minor, infrequent and unlikely to disrupt others, such as a brief sigh or doodle. Attention can sometimes reward the very behavior you want to stop. The hard part is judging whether the behavior is truly minor; if it spreads, the ripple effect makes ignoring a mistake.

**Gesturing nonverbally** is the next step: eye contact, a raised eyebrow, a finger to the lips, or moving closer to the learner. These redirect behavior with little or no talk and do not interrupt the lesson for everyone else.

Be careful with cultural differences. Young children and learners raised in other cultural communities may have learned different nonverbal signals and may misread yours. Explain your signals explicitly early in the year.
Memory aid: "Ignore the tiny, signal the small, speak only when needed."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 7 Ignoring misbehaviors; Gesturing nonverbally

title: Space, procedures, rules and transitions
md:
Most good classroom management is prevention. Seifert and Sutton describe four tools.

**Arrange space** so learners can focus and distractions are few. Use wall displays to reinforce lessons and show student work, but do not crowd the walls, which makes a room feel busy and small.

Set **procedures**, or routines, for common repeated tasks, such as passing papers or going to the restroom. They are like social conventions, so teachers may simply announce and explain them.

Set a few **rules**, standards of behavior that learners must take personal responsibility for, such as "respect other people's property". Keep them **few and general**. Because rules concern responsibility, there is a stronger case for involving learners in making rules than procedures.
