Plan **transitions** between activities. They waste time and invite misbehavior unless materials are ready and directions are clear.
Memory aid: "Space, Procedures, Rules, Transitions — prevent before you correct."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 7 Arranging classroom space; procedures and routines; classroom rules; Managing transitions

title: Technology in limited and rich classrooms
md:
Many Philippine classrooms have one computer or none, and patchy internet. Seifert and Sutton note that when computers are scarce they are often used only as a "fancy typewriter" or an encyclopedia. Yet even **one classroom computer** can show upcoming assignments, enrich a learner with a special interest, and give extra review to learners who need it.

As technology grows, the teacher's role shifts from **"full-frontal teaching"** to **"guide on the side"**, helping individuals plan and carry out their own learning. But technology has costs. It takes money that might buy books or hire staff, learners need help to tell reliable sites from "fluff", and some activities, such as choral practice or sports, do not suit it.

Two newer uses are **gamification**, adding points, badges, levels and quick feedback to lessons, and **adaptive learning**, in which software adjusts tasks to each learner's answers.
Memory aid: "One computer can still Present, Enrich, Review."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 1 New trend #2; SRC-0146 lead; SRC-0147 lead

title: Kounin's withitness, overlapping and the ripple effect
md:
Jacob **Kounin's** classic classroom studies (1970) gave teachers three useful terms.

**Withitness** is being aware of everything happening in the room at once, like having "eyes in the back of your head". It does not mean giving every activity equal attention, only noticing all of them. Experienced teachers show more withitness than beginners, but it grows with practice.

**Overlapping** is acting on two or more events at nearly the same time, such as helping one group while signaling a wandering learner to sit down. Withitness makes overlapping possible.

The **ripple effect** is the spread of misbehavior: when a small disruption is left alone, others may copy it.

Simply showing learners that you are withit, by scanning the room, moving around and naming what you see, can prevent off-task behavior before it starts.
Memory aid: "With-it sees all; Overlap handles two; Ripple spreads if ignored."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 7 withitness passage; Responding to student misbehavior

title: Attributions, self-efficacy and learned helplessness
md:
How learners explain their results shapes their motivation. Weiner's attribution ideas describe three dimensions.
- **Locus:** internal ("I am good at this") or external ("the test was easy").
- **Stability:** ability is fairly stable; effort is unstable and must be renewed each time.
- **Controllability:** effort is controllable; luck and task difficulty are not.

Teachers should steer learners toward **effort and strategy**, which are internal, unstable and controllable: "You improved because you practiced the steps."

**Self-efficacy**, from Bandura, is the belief that you can carry out a specific task or reach a specific goal. It is like confidence, but tied to a particular task. When self-efficacy is very low, a learner may develop **learned helplessness**, feeling no control at all over success, and stop trying. Small, achievable successes and specific feedback rebuild it.
Memory aid: "Where? How lasting? Can I change it? — praise effort, build efficacy."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 6 attributions; self-efficacy

title: Bandura's observational learning
md:
Albert Bandura showed that people can learn by watching others, not only from their own rewards and punishments. This is observational learning, also called modeling. His work stressed that humans are social. We live, learn and develop among other people, and we both influence them and are influenced by them. In a classroom, the teacher is always a model. A Home Economics teacher who washes hands, sets out tools neatly and handles knives safely teaches those habits by example, often more powerfully than by lecture. Students also learn from peers they watch, which is why showing a good example from a classmate can work. On the exam, a scenario where a learner copies a behavior after seeing someone else do it, and receives no direct reward, points to Bandura.
Memory aid: "Bandura = Behold, then behave."
Sources: SRC-0087 section 1.3; SRC-0086 section 6.4

title: Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems
md:
Urie Bronfenbrenner pictured the child at the center of nested systems.
- **Microsystem:** the settings the child directly experiences, such as family, classmates, teachers and health workers.
- **Mesosystem:** the connections between those settings. A parent–teacher conference is the classic example.
- **Exosystem:** settings the child never enters that still affect them. A parent's new work-from-home policy changes life at home, for instance.
- **Macrosystem:** the widest layer: culture, values, religion, the economy and national laws.
- **Chronosystem:** time. All the layers change together through historical events and life transitions.

A common exam trap mixes up the mesosystem and the exosystem. If two of the child's own settings are talking to each other, it is the mesosystem. If a setting the child is not part of affects the child, it is the exosystem.
Memory aid: "My Mom Expects Many Chores" — Micro, Meso, Exo, Macro, Chrono.
Sources: SRC-0087 section 1.4

title: Classical conditioning (Pavlov)
md:
Ivan Pavlov discovered classical conditioning while studying digestion in dogs. Meat powder is an unconditioned stimulus because it naturally makes dogs salivate, and that salivation is an unconditioned response. A tone at first means nothing to the dog, so it is a neutral stimulus. Pavlov sounded the tone just before giving the meat powder, again and again. Eventually the tone alone made the dogs salivate. The tone had become a conditioned stimulus, and the salivation to it a conditioned response. Classroom versions are common. A learner who was embarrassed during recitation may feel anxious whenever their name is called. Classical conditioning pairs two stimuli and works on reflexes and feelings. Operant conditioning, by contrast, works through the consequences of a chosen behavior.
Memory aid: "Pavlov Pairs" — pairing a signal with something that already triggers a reflex.
Sources: SRC-0086 section 6.2; SRC-0087 section 1.3

title: Erikson's psychosocial stages
md:
Erik Erikson updated Freud's ideas into a psychosocial theory with eight stages across the whole lifespan. Each stage is a crisis between the person and society.
- **Trust vs mistrust (0–1):** will my needs be met?
- **Autonomy vs shame and doubt (1–3):** can I do things myself?
- **Initiative vs guilt (3–6):** taking initiative in activities.
- **Industry vs inferiority (7–11):** am I competent?
- **Identity vs confusion (12–18):** who am I?
- **Intimacy vs isolation (19–29):** close relationships.
- **Generativity vs stagnation (30–64):** contributing to society and family.
- **Integrity vs despair (65 and over):** making sense of one's life.

A secondary teacher works mainly with learners in the identity stage. Activities that let students explore roles, values and future careers support that task.
Memory aid: "TAI-II-GI" — Trust, Autonomy, Initiative, Industry, Identity, Intimacy, Generativity, Integrity.
Sources: SRC-0087 section 1.3, Table 1.1

title: Freud's psychosexual stages
md:
Sigmund Freud proposed five psychosexual stages: oral (0–1, weaning), anal (1–3, toilet training), phallic (3–6), latency (6–12) and genital (12 and up). Freud's theory matters historically because later theorists built on it. Erik Erikson, for example, trained in psychoanalysis and turned Freud's ideas into a psychosocial theory covering the whole lifespan. Modern psychology, however, does not support most of Freud's specific claims, and psychologists dispute the psychosexual stages as an explanation of personality. For the exam, know the order of the five stages and that Freud's theory is psychosexual while Erikson's is psychosocial. Do not confuse the counts. Freud has five stages that end in adolescence. Erikson has eight that continue into old age.
Memory aid: "Old Angry Pirates Love Gold" — Oral, Anal, Phallic, Latency, Genital.
Sources: SRC-0086 sections 9.2 and 11.2 (Table 11.1); SRC-0087 section 1.3

title: Gardner's multiple intelligences
md:
Howard Gardner, a Harvard psychologist and former student of Erik Erikson, proposed that each person has at least eight intelligences. They are linguistic, logical-mathematical, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, spatial, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic. Interpersonal intelligence means understanding other people. Intrapersonal means understanding oneself. Bodily-kinesthetic covers skilled movement, which matters in cooking and sewing. The theory is popular with educators because it suggests everyone can be smart in some way. But cognitive psychologists heavily criticize it for lacking empirical evidence. For teaching, the useful lesson is to offer varied tasks, such as hands-on work, discussion, visuals and reflection, rather than to label children as one type. On the exam, expect to match a description to the right intelligence. The pair interpersonal and intrapersonal is the classic trap.
Memory aid: "Inter = between people; intra = inside me."
Sources: SRC-0086 section 7.4

title: Kohlberg's levels of moral reasoning
md:
Lawrence Kohlberg extended Piaget's work on moral reasoning. He gave people dilemmas such as the Heinz dilemma, where a husband steals an overpriced drug to save his dying wife. He scored the reasoning, not the yes or no answer. He found three levels.
- **Pre-conventional:** common before about age nine or ten. Choices rest on consequences to oneself: avoiding punishment, obeying, or getting a reward.
- **Conventional:** from early adolescence. People judge by what others will think, or by rules and laws that keep order.
- **Post-conventional:** reached only after formal operational thinking, and by only a few people. Reasoning rests on internalized principles such as justice and compassion, even when these conflict with the law.

If a student says "stealing is wrong because you will get caught," that is pre-conventional. "Because people will think you are a thief" is conventional.
Memory aid: "Me, then We, then Principle."
Sources: SRC-0086 section 9.2; SRC-0087 section 8.2

title: Motivation — intrinsic, extrinsic, Maslow's hierarchy
md:
Motivation is what directs behavior toward a goal. Intrinsic motivation comes from inside, from the satisfaction of the task itself. Extrinsic motivation is about getting something from others, such as grades, prizes or praise. Abraham Maslow, in 1943, arranged needs in a hierarchy, usually drawn as a pyramid.
1. Physiological needs for survival, such as food, water and sleep (the base).
2. Safety and security.
3. Love and belonging.
4. Esteem, meaning self-worth and confidence.
5. Self-actualization, reaching one's full potential, at the top.

Maslow held that the top can be reached only when the lower needs are met. That is the logic behind school feeding programs and a safe, welcoming classroom: a hungry, frightened or excluded learner struggles to focus on lessons.
Memory aid: "Feed, Shield, Belong, Respect, Become."
Sources: SRC-0086 section 10.1

title: Information processing — Atkinson-Shiffrin memory model
md:
The information processing view compares the mind to a computer. Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin proposed in 1968 that information passes through three stages before it is stored for good.
1. **Sensory memory:** a very brief hold on everything we see and hear. Only what we attend to moves on.
2. **Short-term memory:** a small, temporary store that works on incoming information and links it to what we already know. It is a component of working memory, and the two terms are not exactly the same.
3. **Long-term memory:** continuous storage with a capacity believed to be unlimited.

For teaching, this explains why attention comes first, why new information should connect to prior knowledge, and why practice and retrieval help move learning into long-term memory.
Memory aid: "See it, hold it, keep it" — sensory, short-term, long-term.
Sources: SRC-0086 section 8.1

title: Operant conditioning (Skinner), reinforcement and punishment
md:
B. F. Skinner built on Thorndike's law of effect: consequences change how often a behavior happens. Reinforcement makes a behavior more likely, and punishment makes it less likely. "Positive" means something is added, and "negative" means something is removed.
- Praising a student for finished homework is positive reinforcement.
- Excusing a student from a quiz because they joined every activity removes something unpleasant to increase participation. That is negative reinforcement, not punishment.
- Extra chores for misbehaving is positive punishment.
- Taking away recess is negative punishment.

Reinforcement can follow different schedules. A variable-ratio schedule rewards after an unpredictable number of responses, as in gambling. It produces a high, steady rate of behavior and the slowest extinction once rewards stop.
Memory aid: "Reinforce rises, punish drops; plus adds, minus takes."
Sources: SRC-0086 section 6.3, Tables 6.2–6.3; SRC-0087 section 1.3

title: Piaget's stages of cognitive development
md:
Jean Piaget described four stages of thinking.
- **Sensorimotor (about 0–2):** babies learn through their senses and actions and develop object permanence, the knowledge that things still exist when hidden.
- **Preoperational (about 2–6 or 7):** children use words and images and enjoy pretend play, but their reasoning is not yet logical and they are egocentric, finding it hard to take another person's view.
- **Concrete operational (about 7–11):** children reason logically about real, concrete things and master conservation, for example that pouring water into a taller glass does not change the amount.
- **Formal operational (about 12 and up):** abstract and hypothetical reasoning becomes possible.

Most high school learners are in the last stage, so "what if" problems, debates and moral reasoning suit them. Exam items test the order and the hallmark of each stage more than the exact edge ages.
Memory aid: "Smart Penguins Count Fish" — Sensorimotor, Preoperational, Concrete, Formal.
Sources: SRC-0087 section 1.3, Table 1.2

title: Intrinsic/extrinsic motivation, goals, self-determination, TARGET
md:
**Intrinsic motivation** comes from within, such as enjoying sewing for its own sake. **Extrinsic motivation** comes from outside, such as grades or prizes. **Self-determination theory** says these are not opposites but a **continuum**, and motivation grows when three needs are met: **autonomy** (feeling free to choose), **competence** (feeling capable) and **relatedness** (feeling connected to others). Teachers support competence with tasks that are challenging but achievable.

Goals matter too. **Mastery goals**, aiming to learn and improve, sustain interest better than **performance goals**, aiming to look better than others, which can breed unhealthy competition.

Carole **Ames's TARGET** model gathers these ideas into six areas a teacher controls: **Task**, **Authority** (sharing choices), **Recognition**, **Grouping**, **Evaluation** and **Time**.
Memory aid: "Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness; aim for mastery; TARGET = Task, Authority, Recognition, Grouping, Evaluation, Time."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 6 self-determination; goals; TARGET

title: Learners with special needs and cognitive styles
md:
Seifert and Sutton note that the most common special need is a **learning disability**: an impairment in a specific aspect of learning, especially **reading**. **ADHD**, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, is a problem with **sustaining attention and controlling impulses**. Less common are speech and language disorders and cognitive disabilities.

Inclusive teaching asks three things of teachers: provide **alternative ways of assessment**, arrange a learning environment that is as normal, or **least restrictive**, as possible, and help create **individual educational plans (IEPs)**. (See PE-A1 for RA 11650, the Philippine inclusion law.)

Learners also differ in **cognitive style**. **Field-dependent** learners perceive things globally and often like working with others; **field-independent** learners prefer analytic tasks and working alone. Be careful with the label "learning styles": people are less consistent across situations than the term suggests.
Memory aid: "LD = specific skill, ADHD = attention and impulse; Assess differently, Least restrictive, IEP."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 5; Ch. 4

title: Vygotsky — ZPD and scaffolding
md:
Lev Vygotsky argued that thinking develops through social interaction, not only through a child's solo discovery. His best-known idea is the zone of proximal development, or ZPD. It holds concepts and skills just beyond what a learner can do alone, which the learner is ready to master with a little help, often from a teacher, a parent or a more skilled peer. That help is called scaffolding. Like training wheels on a bicycle, it is given while the learner needs it and then gradually withdrawn as the learner becomes competent. In a Home Economics class, a teacher who demonstrates a stitch, guides the student through the first few, and then steps back is scaffolding inside the ZPD. Remember the difference: the ZPD is the zone of possible learning; scaffolding is the support used within it.
Memory aid: "Zone = where; scaffold = how (and then remove it)."
Sources: SRC-0087 section 1.3

title: Mean, median and mode
md:
Measures of central tendency describe a typical score.
- **Mean:** add all scores and divide by how many there are.
- **Median:** the middle score when scores are in order; half are above and half below.
- **Mode:** the most frequent score. Two modes make a distribution **bimodal**.

Each tells you something different. The mean is used in further statistics, but it is **pulled by extreme scores**, called outliers. The median is **not**.

Example: ten quiz scores are 4, 18, 18, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 20 and 20. The mean is 175 divided by 10, or 17.5, dragged down by the single 4. The median and the mode are both 19, which better describes most of the class. So when a few scores are extreme, the median is often the better summary of typical performance.

In a perfectly normal, bell-shaped distribution, the mean, median and mode are equal.
Memory aid: "Mean = average, Median = middle, Mode = most; outliers move only the mean."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 12 Central tendency and variability; The normal distribution

title: Completion, short-answer and essay items
md:
**Constructed response** items ask learners to recall and produce an answer, so guessing drops.

**Completion** and **short-answer** items are nearly the same. Completion gives a statement with a blank; short answer asks a direct question. Both are answered with a word, phrase, number or symbol, and they are common in mathematics, such as "If x = 6, what is x(x − 1)?". Write them so only one answer fits.

**Extended response**, or essay, items ask for a paragraph or more. Their main strength is measuring **complex outcomes**, especially integration and application, and they also show writing skill. They seem easy to write, but good prompts that match the outcome are hard. A clear prompt states the task and may give planning notes, such as the points to cover.

Essays are hard to score reliably. Use a **scoring rubric** or point scheme.
Memory aid: "Short = one right word; Essay = complex thinking, needs a rubric."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Constructed response items; Completion and short answer; Extended response; Scoring rubrics

title: Giving feedback on assessment
md:
Feedback turns assessment into learning. Seifert and Sutton give three guidelines.

**Make it prompt.** The longer the gap between the work and the feedback, the longer learners keep their misconceptions, and the less they remember what they were thinking when they did the task.

**Make it specific.** Tell learners clearly what they did well and what needs changing. Comments like "good work" or "needs improvement" do not show how to improve. A well-designed rubric helps by naming strengths and weaknesses criterion by criterion.

**Keep the grade from drowning the message.** Grades are often required, but placing the grade after the comments, or on the last page, helps learners read the comments first. Letting learners keep grades private also reduces comparison.

When reporting to parents, the same rule applies: describe what the child can do and what to work on next, not only the number.
Memory aid: "Fast, Specific, Comments before grade."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Providing feedback

title: Writing good multiple-choice items
md:
**Multiple choice** is the most used objective format because it can test higher thinking, such as application, not just facts. With four or five options, guessing is lower than in true-false, and it does not need the homogeneous lists matching requires.

Writing one well takes three steps.
1. **State the problem clearly in the stem.** If the options are unrelated statements, the item is really several true-false items.
2. **Write plausible alternatives.** Wrong options should be believable to learners who have not mastered the content, and all options should fit the stem grammatically.
3. **Remove irrelevant clues.** Do not make the correct option the longest one. Do not cluster answers in position b or c; use every position about equally, but not in an exact pattern. Avoid negatives and double negatives, and avoid trivial questions.

This very question bank checks answer length and position for these reasons.
Memory aid: "Clear stem, plausible distractors, no clues."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Common problems; Strengths and weaknesses; Table 37

title: Norm-referenced vs criterion-referenced interpretation
md:
The same test score can be read in two ways.

A **criterion-referenced** interpretation compares a learner with a **standard**. It describes what the learner can or cannot do: "Alisha mastered 65 percent of the Grade 2 problems." Mastery checks, competency assessments and most classroom quizzes work this way.

A **norm-referenced** interpretation compares a learner with **other learners**, the norm group. It reports rank, such as a percentile: "Alisha scored higher than 75 percent of the norm group." Entrance tests and ranking for honors use this logic.

For planning instruction, teachers usually need to know what learners can and cannot do, so **criterion-referenced** information is generally more useful. Standards-based accountability also relies mostly on criterion-referenced tests. Norm-referenced tests are now used more for diagnosis and placement, for example of learners with special needs.
Memory aid: "Criterion = against the Content; Norm = against the Neighbors."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 12 Basic concepts

title: The normal curve and percentiles
md:
Many large sets of scores form a **normal distribution**: a symmetric bell with most scores near the middle and fewer at the extremes. In it, the mean, median and mode are the same.

The normal curve links standard deviations to percentages. About **34 percent** of scores lie between the mean and one SD above it, and another 34 percent between the mean and one SD below. So about **68 percent** fall within one SD of the mean. About **14 percent** lie between one and two SDs above the mean, and only about **2 percent** lie beyond two SDs above.

Percentiles follow. A learner at the mean is at the **50th percentile**. A learner one SD above the mean is at about the **84th percentile**, because 50 plus 34 percent of scores are below. On an IQ test (mean 100, SD 15), 115 is about the 84th percentile.
Memory aid: "34–14–2 each side; mean = 50th, +1 SD = 84th."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 12 The normal distribution

title: Reliability and bias
md:
**Reliability** is consistency: would learners get similar scores if they took the assessment again, or if a different teacher scored it? Teachers can raise reliability in three ways. Use **more items or tasks**, since one confusing item changes a 5-item score by 20 percent but a 50-item score by only 2 percent. Write **clear directions and tasks**. Use **clear scoring criteria**, such as rubrics.

**Bias** occurs when parts of an assessment distort performance because of learners' gender, ethnicity or social class. It comes in two forms. **Offensiveness** uses negative stereotypes, such as showing all doctors as men and all nurses as women. **Unfair penalization** depends on background experiences some groups lack, such as a math problem built around a sport only some learners know.

Low scores alone do not prove bias. And a test can be reliable without being valid: it can consistently measure the wrong thing.
Memory aid: "More items, clear tasks, clear criteria — no stereotypes, no unfair background."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Reliability; Absence of bias

title: True-false and matching items
md:
**Selected response** items ask learners to recognize an answer the teacher provides. They are called **objective** because scoring does not depend on the scorer's judgment, which raises reliability. But using only objective tests can lower validity, because they do not fit every learning goal.

**True-false** items suit facts such as vocabulary, formulas, dates, names and technical terms. They are quick to answer and easy to write, but learners have a **50 percent chance** of guessing correctly, so scores are hard to interpret.

**Matching** items use two parallel columns, such as terms and definitions. Put **more choices in the answer column** than in the premise column, so one mistake does not force another. Matching works for lower-level knowledge, but the lists must be **homogeneous**, all about one kind of thing, which is harder than it looks.

Common flaws in both: unclear wording, copied textbook sentences, negatives, and trivial content.
Memory aid: "True-false: fast but 50–50; Matching: extra answers, same kind."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Selected response items; Common problems; Strengths and weaknesses

title: z-scores, T-scores, stanines and grade equivalents
md:
A **standard score** reports a result in standard-deviation units from the mean.

The **z-score** has mean 0 and SD 1: z = (score − mean) ÷ SD. If the mean is 100 and the SD is 15, a score of 130 gives z = (130 − 100) ÷ 15 = 2, two SDs above the mean. A negative z means below the mean.

The **T-score** has mean 50 and SD 10, so T = 50 + 10z. A T-score of 70 equals z = 2.

**Stanines** use a nine-point scale with mean 5 and SD 2, reported only as whole numbers.

A **grade-equivalent** score such as 3.7 means performance typical of a Grade 3 learner in the seventh month. It is easily misread: a Grade 4 learner scoring 6.0 performed on the Grade 4 test as a Grade 6 learner would, not that the child can do Grade 6 work.
Memory aid: "z 0/1, T 50/10, Stanine 5/2."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 12 Kinds of test scores; Grade equivalent scores

title: Validity
md:
**Validity** asks whether the interpretations and uses of assessment results are justified. Strictly, validity belongs to the meaning drawn from scores, and it is a matter of degree: high, moderate or low.

There are three main sources of validity evidence.
- **Content validity:** Does the assessment cover the content and tasks it should? A midterm on chapters 1 to 7 should sample all seven chapters, not only the last four, and only content from that course.
- **Construct validity:** Does it measure the intended ability and not something else? A math-reasoning test written in difficult English may measure English proficiency for recent immigrants, not math.
- **Criterion-related or predictive validity:** Do scores predict later performance? Admission tests are judged by how well they predict first-year grades.

A practical rule: align the assessment with the goal. If the goal is to cook a dish, have learners cook it.
Memory aid: "Content covers, Construct targets, Criterion predicts."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Validity; Selected response items

title: Range, variance and standard deviation
md:
Two classes can have the same mean but very different spreads, so teachers also measure **variability**.

The **range** is the highest score minus the lowest score. It is quick, but it uses only two scores, so one unusual score can change it a lot.

The **standard deviation (SD)** uses every score. It shows how far, on average, scores lie from the mean. To compute it: find the mean; subtract the mean from each score; square each deviation; average the squared deviations, which gives the **variance**; then take the square root of the variance to get the SD.

A small SD means scores cluster near the mean, so the class performed similarly. A large SD means scores are spread out, so the class is more varied and may need more differentiated teaching.
Memory aid: "Range = top minus bottom; SD = average distance from the mean (square, average, root)."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 12 Central tendency and variability; Calculating a standard deviation

title: Gibbs' reflective cycle and Brookfield's lenses
md:
Two models give reflection a structure.

**Gibbs' reflective cycle (1988)** has six stages. **Description:** what happened? **Feelings:** what were you thinking and feeling? **Evaluation:** what was good and bad? **Analysis:** what sense can you make of it? **Conclusion:** what else could you have done? **Action plan:** what will you do next time? It turns a vague "the lesson went badly" into a plan.

**Stephen Brookfield (1998)** says critically reflective teachers check their assumptions through **four lenses**. First, their own **autobiography as learners**. Second, their **learners' eyes**, which often reveal surprising interpretations of what the teacher meant. Third, **colleagues' experiences**, which act as critical mirrors. Fourth, **theoretical literature**, which helps name what seemed like personal problems.

An internship reflection paper that uses student feedback and a theory reading is using two of Brookfield's lenses.
Memory aid: "Gibbs: Don't Forget Every Amazing Class Activity; Brookfield: Me, Them, Peers, Theory."
Sources: SRC-0189 Gibbs 1988; Brookfield 1998

title: Kolb's experiential learning cycle
md:
Field study and internship rest on **experiential learning**: learning from direct experience that is then reflected on and used. **David Kolb**, influenced by Dewey, Piaget and Lewin, described it as a four-stage cycle.
1. **Concrete experience:** you do something, such as observing a Grade 8 cookery class.
2. **Reflective observation:** you look back on it. What happened? What did learners do?
3. **Abstract conceptualization:** you make sense of it by linking it to ideas or theory, for example noticing that the teacher's demonstration fits Bandura's modeling.
4. **Active experimentation:** you try out what you learned, such as planning your own demonstration, which becomes a new concrete experience.

Kolb's framework stresses that experience alone is not enough. The learner must be willing to take part, able to reflect, able to conceptualize, and able to make decisions and solve problems. It also needs an intention to learn.
Memory aid: "Every Rider Can Experiment" = Experience, Reflect, Conceptualize, Experiment.
Sources: SRC-0188 Kolb's model, Elements, Implementation; SRC-0189 Kolb

title: Microteaching
md:
**Microteaching** is a teacher-training technique invented in **1963 at Stanford University** by **Dwight W. Allen**. It simplifies the complex job of teaching so one skill can be practiced and improved.

In the original form, a trainee prepared a **short lesson**, usually about **20 minutes**, for a **small group** of learners. The lesson was **video-recorded**. Afterwards the trainee, fellow trainees, a master teacher and the learners watched the recording together and commented on what worked and what could improve, with reference to the lesson's objectives. The trainee could then reteach.

Everything is **scaled down**: class size, time, task and content. That makes feedback specific, for example on questioning or giving directions. John Hattie's review of research found microteaching among the most effective methods for improving student outcomes.

In teacher education, microteaching usually comes before full teaching internship.
Memory aid: "Small class, short lesson, recorded, reviewed, retaught."
Sources: SRC-0190 lead, Techniques

title: Sources of professional learning and reflection
md:
Reflection is personal, since only you lived your teaching experiences, but it grows faster with others. Seifert and Sutton group resources for professional learning into four kinds.
1. **Talking and collaborating with colleagues.** One-to-one conversations about teaching allow full participation and some confidentiality. **Group study**, where teachers meet to learn a new curriculum or plan school-wide activities, is especially good for beginning teachers learning from veterans.
2. **Professional associations**, which publish journals and hold meetings.
3. **Workshops and conferences**, which bring wider expertise than one school, though they cost time and money.
4. **Reading professional literature**, while asking what each study's purpose is and how it applies to your own class.

The conversations must be about educational matters to help. Teachers can also add to professional knowledge themselves through **action research**.
Memory aid: "Colleagues, Associations, Conferences, Literature — CACL."
Sources: SRC-0109 Appendix C Types of resources; Colleagues as a resource

title: Schön's reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action
md:
**Donald Schön's** book *The Reflective Practitioner* (1983) explained how professionals improve through a kind of practiced improvisation. He described two types of reflection.

**Reflection-in-action** happens **while** you are acting. A student teacher sees puzzled faces during a demonstration, realizes the steps are too fast, and slows down and adds a visual on the spot.

**Reflection-on-action** happens **after** the event. That evening, the same student teacher writes in a journal about what went wrong, what went right, and what to do differently next time.

For Schön, professional growth begins when a practitioner starts to **doubt** his or her own actions and to frame situations as problems to solve, rather than accepting routines without question. Field study journals, post-observation conferences and video review all build both kinds of reflection.
Memory aid: "In = during the lesson; On = after the lesson."
Sources: SRC-0189 lead; Schön

title: Student teaching and its supervisors
md:
**Student teaching**, also called teaching practice, is a supervised instructional experience. It is usually the **culminating course** of a pre-service teacher education program and lasts about one school term, long enough to complete the college's required tasks.

The student teacher is placed in a cooperating school and supervised on two sides. The **cooperating teacher** is the experienced, licensed teacher in the host school whose class the student teacher shares and eventually takes over. The **college supervisor** comes from the teacher education institution, observes and evaluates, and serves as the **liaison** between the cooperating teacher and the college's student-teaching office.

Student teaching differs from a **practicum**, which in some systems is for teachers who already hold a license and want to add another specialization. Both are college-supervised, field-based experiences.

On the LET, "Who is the student teacher's immediate mentor in the school?" points to the cooperating teacher.
Memory aid: "Cooperating teacher in the classroom; College supervisor connects the college."
Sources: SRC-0191 lead

title: Portfolios in field study and internship
md:
Field study and internship usually end with a **portfolio**. Seifert and Sutton define a portfolio as a meaningful, **purposeful** collection of work that tells the story of achievement or growth, not just a folder of everything.

They describe four pairs of choices, useful for designing a teaching portfolio.
- **For learning vs of learning:** reflection and self-chosen entries, or evidence to certify completion.
- **Progress vs current accomplishment:** drafts and early lesson plans that show growth, or only recent finished work.
- **Showcase vs documentation:** your best lessons and reflections, or every observation sheet and plan.
- **Working vs finished:** a day-to-day collection for developing ideas, or a polished version for an audience, such as a job interview.

A strong intern portfolio pairs artifacts, such as lesson plans, learner work and observation notes, with written **reflections** explaining what each shows.
Memory aid: "Purposeful, not everything: For/Of, Growth/Now, Best/All, Working/Finished."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Portfolios

title: Assumptions behind action research; Lewin's spiral
md:
The term **action research** was coined by **Kurt Lewin** in 1944. He described it as a **spiral of steps**, each a circle of **planning, action and fact-finding** about the result of the action. Each turn of the spiral leads to new planning.

Seifert and Sutton list four ideas that most action research studies share.
1. **Teaching is itself a form of research.** Every lesson tests ideas about how learners learn.
2. **Action research requires substantial reflection**, just as good teaching does.
3. **Collaboration** among teachers is crucial, both to make the research meaningful and to improve teaching.
4. **Teachers' knowledge should be shared publicly**, especially when it was gained systematically.

So a teacher who quietly tries a new seating plan is reflecting; a teacher who plans it, collects data, studies the results, and presents them at a school learning session is doing action research.
Memory aid: "Lewin's spiral: Plan, Act, Find out — and teachers Research, Reflect, Collaborate, Share."
Sources: SRC-0109 Appendix C Action research in practice; SRC-0169 lead

title: Data collection and analysis in action research
md:
Action research data come from ordinary classroom life, gathered more systematically. Seifert and Sutton's examples include: **assessing students' assignments**; **observing** students as they work; **interviewing** students about their experiences; **videotaping** your own lessons; and keeping a **journal diary** of your observations.

Analysis looks for **patterns**: common strengths and problems across several students, or differences in how you interact with different groups. The teacher then tries a change and watches what happens. Results are shared in a brief written or oral report to fellow staff, a summary in the journal, or a talk with students.

A few research-design ideas help interpret results honestly. A comparison or **control group** shows whether change came from the new method. **Lurking variables**, such as a holiday week, can cloud results. A **convenience sample**, like only the learners who stay after class, may be biased.
Memory aid: "Work, Watch, Ask, Record, Write — then look for patterns."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 1 Table 1; SRC-0091 1.2, 1.4

title: Ethics of action research
md:
Action research can create a **conflict of interest**. A teacher's first priority is the **welfare of students**: their learning, motivation and acceptance. A researcher's priority is the topic. Usually these fit together, but not always.

Ethical problems arise when results are made **public**, in a journal, a conference or even informal talk outside the class. Three issues matter.
- **Privacy:** use a **pseudonym** and change identifying details, in any report or hallway conversation, without hiding facts essential to the study.
- **Informed consent:** if data will be shared outside the school community, get permission from parents or guardians and the students, using a form that describes the study and data, states participation is voluntary, and promises confidentiality or anonymity.
- **Freedom to participate:** learners may decline to be in the research, even though class work itself is required.

The Data Privacy Act also treats education and health data as sensitive.
Memory aid: "PIF — Privacy, Informed consent, Freedom to participate."
Sources: SRC-0109 Appendix C Ethical cautions; Insuring privacy; Ch. 11 Ethical issues; SRC-0045 Sec. 3(l)

title: The action research cycle (Mertler)
md:
Seifert and Sutton describe the action research cycle from Mertler in four stages.

**1. Planning.** First identify and define the problem. It often starts as vague unease and becomes a researchable question, such as "Why do half my learners skip the handwashing step?" Next, **review related literature**, alone, in a study group or in a course. Then write a **research plan**: what data to collect, how and when.

**2. Acting.** Collect and analyze the data. Keep it **manageable**; complex statistics are not required.

**3. Developing an action plan.** Decide on changes, carry them out, and **document** what you did so others can understand it.

**4. Communicating and reflecting.** Share results with colleagues, at a conference or in a teachers' journal, and include students and parents if they took part. Ask: What did I learn? What should I do next? That begins a new cycle.
Memory aid: "Plan, Act, Action plan, Share and Reflect — then spiral again."
Sources: SRC-0109 Ch. 11 Cycles of planning, acting and reflecting

title: What makes research "action research"
md:
**Action research**, also called teacher research, is systematic, intentional inquiry by teachers to **improve their own practice**. It is different from research **about** teaching, which professional researchers design and interpret, often around questions set by academic fields or administrators.

Seifert and Sutton name three defining features. First, action research **starts from real problems** of classroom practice, such as chronic lateness or poor lab safety habits. Second, its findings are about **particular teachers and classrooms**, not teachers in general. Supporters say this makes it more credible as practical guidance, because it fits real classrooms. Third, its main audience is **other teachers**, so it offers an insider's view.

Compared with simply good teaching, action research is planned more carefully, recorded more systematically and shared more openly. That is why it is seen as a mark of teacher professionalism.
Memory aid: "My problem, my class, my colleagues."
Sources: SRC-0109 Appendix C The nature of action research; Ch. 1

title: From findings to recommendations
md:
The TOS asks teachers to **recommend solutions based on research**. That means two skills: reading others' research critically and using your own findings.

When reading research, Seifert and Sutton advise asking what the study's **purpose** is and how useful it is for your own work and goals. Research by professors or administrators may frame questions differently from a classroom teacher, so translate findings to your setting.

When writing up your own action research, a common structure is **IMRaD**: Introduction (the problem and question), Methods (who, what data, how), Results (what you found) and Discussion (what it means, and what to do). Recommendations belong in the Discussion and should follow from the results, not from wishes. For example, if checklists raised handwashing compliance from 50 to 90 percent in three weeks, recommend checklists for all kitchen labs and a follow-up cycle to see if the gain lasts.
Memory aid: "Recommend only what your Results can carry."
Sources: SRC-0109 Appendix C; SRC-0168 lead, Overview
